definition.text: A bias toward keeping things as they currently are, also called default bias.

facts.text: The current state serves as a reference point, so any change from it is felt as a loss or a gain.
It is explained by loss aversion and the endowment effect: the possible losses of switching weigh more than the possible gains.
It differs from a rational preference for the status quo, where the current state really is better, and from simple inertia.
Samuelson and Zeckhauser showed in 1988 that people stick with an option framed as the status quo, and that the pull grows as more alternatives are offered.
In a 1986 retirement study, most people never changed how they split savings between two funds, despite very different returns and no switching costs.
Automatic enrolment in retirement plans, where employees must opt out, uses this bias to raise saving.
Defaults keep their effect even when people are told why the default was chosen.

definition.text: A check for status quo bias: if changing a quantity one way is judged bad, ask whether changing it the other way is also judged bad.

facts.text: If both directions are judged bad, those judging must explain why the current value cannot be improved; if they cannot, status quo bias is suspected.
Its rationale is that of all possible values only a few can be best, so it is unlikely that the current value happens to be one of them.

definition.text: An economic theory of the emotional reward people get from giving to others.

facts.text: In James Andreoni's original model (1989, 1990), people enjoy 'doing their part' whatever the actual impact of their gift.
It describes impure altruism, a mix of altruistic and selfish motives for giving.
Under pure altruism, government grants should fully crowd out private donations; warm glow helps explain why they do not.

Because outside rewards and punishments have often failed to bring lasting green behavior, environmental policy increasingly targets warm glow, with promising results for green energy, recycling and carpooling.
Sustainable investors may get satisfaction from the act itself rather than its impact, so their utility does not rise in line with impact.
A meta-analysis of 36 brain-imaging studies found the brain's reward networks consistently active when people choose to give.
Andreoni himself called adding warm glow to the model 'an admittedly ad hoc fix'.
